title: Black, white and mixed audiences in Armstrong's early jobs
summary: Perdido Street for black audiences, Red Onion mixed, Segretto's white; he never worked Pete Lala's.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Now, was Louie playing, and of course, obviously, I mean, this may be an obvious question, was he playing when he worked in New Orleans? Did he work for both black and white audiences?
Yeah. No, he was... Well, of course, he worked outside a lot, and when he was working on the, on the, uh, you know, in the Marable band, he was playing for exclusively white audiences.
Yeah, I know in Marable, he would have been all white. Yeah. But when he was working in saloons, would that necessarily have all been black?

Well, if he was working over there on Perdido Street, he was working for black audiences. Yeah. If he was working in Red Onion, he'd have been working for mixed audiences. Uh-huh. That was about the only place in town. Yeah. And, uh, if he, he never worked in Pete Lala's or any place like that. Uh, but in, in Segretto's, he was just working with a piano player. Yeah. And, and that was for a white audience.
And that was on, that was on Perdido. On Perdido Street, yeah.
That's been replaced by City Hall. Yeah, right.
